title: Infra modules, GPU fleet, and CI/CD playbook
author: Ava Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook centralizes operational standards and runbook-level guidance for Redwood Inference infrastructure engineering: Terraform/IaC modules, cloud accounts and networking, CI/CD and build patterns, and GPU fleet capacity handling. It is intended for infra engineers, platform owners, SREs supporting model-serving, and new hires onboarding to infra responsibilities.

Scope and intended audience

- Scope: reusable Terraform modules, account/role standards, CI/CD pipelines for infra artifacts, GPU fleet capacity policies and autoscaling patterns, and runbooks for common incidents.
- Audience: infra engineers, platform SREs, release engineers, on-call responders.

Key principles

1) Declarative and auditable infrastructure: use Terraform modules for all cloud resources, require PR reviews for module changes, store state in remote backend with encryption.
2) Small, composable modules: modules should be single-purpose and composable across environments (hosted, dedicated, private).
3) Observability and SLO alignment: every service that impacts inference (routing, scheduler, GPU agents) has latency/cost SLOs and dashboards.
4) Safety for GPU workloads: capacity gating, preemption awareness, and automated fallback policies to preserve customer SLOs.

Ownership and Contacts

- infra-modules (Terraform/IaC): ownership: infra-team-modules (primary: @Diego Martinez).
- GPU fleet and capacity: ownership: gpu-fleet-team (primary: @Priya Nair).
- CI/CD pipelines for infra: ownership: ci-build-team (primary: @Samir Gupta).

Naming and tagging standards (required)

Every cloud resource MUST include the following tags/labels:
- redwood:team = <team-name>
- redwood:env = prod|staging|dev
- redwood:owner = <email>
- redwood:service = <service-key> (e.g., model-serving, batch-ingest)
- billing:cost_center = <cost-center-id>

Example resource name patterns:
- VPCs: rwd-vpc-<env>-<region>
- GPU node pools: rwd-gpu-pool-<env>-<gpu-class>-<region>
- IAM role names: rwd-<service>-role-<env>

Terraform / IaC module standards

- Module layout: every module must include: README.md, examples/, inputs.tf, outputs.tf, variables.tf, versions.tf, CHANGELOG.md.
- Semantic versioning: tag modules with semver; breaking changes require major bump and design doc/ADR.
- Backends: all state is in the centralized Terraform Cloud (or backend: s3 with state locking); state files must be encrypted and access-controlled.
- Testing: each module must have a lightweight integration test in CI that applies to a disposable environment (example: apply a minimal example workspace and run basic resource checks).

Recommended base modules (examples)

- rwd-network-vpc: VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT, VPC endpoints. Inputs: cidr_block, private_subnets_count, enable_flow_logs. Outputs: vpc_id, private_subnet_ids.
- rwd-gke-cluster / rwd-eks-cluster: managed k8s cluster for control plane services. Inputs: node_pool_configs, oauth_settings. Outputs: kubeconfig, cluster_name.
- rwd-gpu-node-pool: managed node pool configured for GPU instance types, preinstalled drivers, nvidia-docker, and placement groups. Inputs: gpu_type, desired_count, taints, labels. Outputs: node_pool_id, autoscaler_policy_id.
- rwd-iam-roles: service roles and policies with least privilege templates.

Example inputs/outputs table (text representation)

| Module | Key inputs | Key outputs |
| rwd-gpu-node-pool | gpu_type, desired_count, taints, labels | node_pool_id, scaling_policy_id |
| rwd-network-vpc | cidr_block, az_count, enable_flow_logs | vpc_id, private_subnet_ids |

Sample Terraform snippet (module usage)

```hcl
module "gpu_pool_prod" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//rwd-gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.2.0"
  gpu_type = "nvidia-a100"
  desired_count = 12
  taints = { gpu=true: "NoSchedule" }
  labels = { service = "model-serving" }
}
```

CI/CD and build patterns for infra artifacts

Goals: safe automated plan/apply, reproducible module releases, gating for breaking changes, and integration tests that run in ephemeral workspaces.

Pipeline components (recommended):
- lint: terraform fmt / tflint / checkov security scan.
- plan: terraform plan in a disposable workspace with PR comment including plan summary.
- policy check: run OPA/Constrains, required tags, network policy checks.
- integration test: run example apply in ephemeral project (minimal resources) and run test assertions.
- publish: on merge to main, tag module, build release artifact, and update module registry.
- apply: apply to long-lived environment workspaces only after approvals from owners and security.

Example CI snippet (pseudocode)

```yaml
stages: [lint, plan, test, publish]
steps:
  - name: terraform-fmt-check
    run: terraform fmt -check
  - name: plan
    run: terraform init && terraform plan -out=plan.out
  - name: policy-eval
    run: opa eval -f pretty "data.redwood.policies.deny"

```

Release policy

- Patch-level changes: automatic publish after merge to main.
- Minor-level changes: require module-owner approval.
- Major/breaking changes: require ADR + cross-team reviewers + scheduled rollout.

GPU fleet and capacity management

Objectives: maintain capacity to meet 99th-percentile latency SLOs while optimizing cost through autoscaling, batching and multitenant packing.

SLOs and thresholds (example - apply per-customer SLA)
- Model-serving tail latency (95p generation): <= 250ms (internal infra metric).
- Queue length threshold for scaling up: > 50 pending requests for > 30s.
- Node utilization target: 60-80% GPU utilization for on-demand pools.
- Preemptible spot pool max fraction: 30% of total capacity for non-latency-critical workloads.

Autoscaling patterns

- Horizontal scaling (preferred): increase node pool size when GPU memory pressure and queue length exceed thresholds.
- Vertical scaling (node type swap): use rolling migration to larger GPU class for predictable throughput increases; schedule during low traffic windows and follow rollout policy.
- Multi-pool routing: route high-priority requests to reserved pools; route best-effort/batch jobs to spot/preemptible pools with eviction fallback logic.

Scaling policy example (text table)

| Condition | Action | Owner | Notes |
| Queue > 50 for 30s | Add +2 nodes to prod GPU pool | gpu-fleet-team | consider warm-up time for driver initialization |
| GPU mem > 85% for 2 minutes | Trigger auto-scale up policy | gpu-fleet-team | avoid oscillation via cooldown 5m |

Warm-up and prewarming

- New nodes must run a prewarm job that pulls container images, initializes NVidia drivers, and preloads common model weights if configured. This reduces cold-start latency.
- Prewarm images are defined in rwd-gpu-node-pool module as prewarm_image and prewarm_jobs_count.

Runbooks and incident response (GPU capacity and networking)

Runbook: GPU capacity shortage (high-level)

1) Detection: alert fires when QueueLength > 100 OR average GPU util > 95% for 5m.
2) Initial responder (L1): confirm alerts in dashboards (Grafana), check autoscaler activity and cloud provider console for failed preemptible allocations.
3) Triage steps (ordered):
   a) Verify autoscaler logs: `kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler`
   b) Check recent pod evictions: `kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -n serving`
   c) If autoscaler inactive, run `terraform apply -target=module.gpu_pool` in a disposable workspace with approver.
   d) If scaling blocked by quota, open cloud quota request and fall back traffic to lower-cost model variants (see traffic-shift playbook).
4) Mitigation: temporarily increase reserved pool or redirect traffic to hosted fallback model endpoint.
5) Post-incident: run postmortem, update capacity targets, and schedule capacity purchase or cluster resize as needed.

Runbook: VPC connectivity issue affecting model-serving

1) Detection: high 5xx rate and service health checks failing across region.
2) Immediate checks: check VPC route tables, NAT gateway status, and security group changes in last 30m.
3) Remediation steps: rollback recent Terraform apply for network changes, reattach routing tables, or failover to secondary region.

Oncall and escalation

- Pager rotation: infra-oncall (primary, secondary, tertiary). Primary for first 30 minutes; if not resolved escalates to secondary, then to engineering manager.
- Escalation contacts: list in team wiki and on Slack #infra-oncall.
- Severity definitions: Sev1 (prod outage affecting >10% traffic), Sev2 (degraded perf > SLOs), Sev3 (minor issue).

Capacity planning and forecasting

Formula (simplified):
Required GPUs = ceil((expected_concurrent_infer_requests * avg_tokens_per_request * token_throughput_per_gpu) / (gpu_efficiency_factor * target_utilization))

- token_throughput_per_gpu: measured in tokens/sec for a representative model on the GPU class.
- gpu_efficiency_factor: accounts for packing inefficiency and variance (suggested 0.7).
- target_utilization: target 0.7.

Example: expected_concurrent = 1000, avg_tokens = 50, token_throughput_per_gpu = 2000 tokens/sec => required = ceil((1000 * 50 / 2000) / (0.7 * 0.7)) = 51 GPUs (round up and add buffer +10%).

Telemetry and dashboards (must-haves)

- GPU pool health dashboard: node counts, GPU utilization, memory pressure, prewarm job success.
- Request queueing dashboard: per-route queue length, latency percentiles, and failed requests.
- Autoscaler dashboard: actions taken, cooldown periods, failure reasons.

Appendix A — Example: CI job that runs a module integration test

```bash
# CI: run example deploy into ephemeral workspace
export TF_WORKSPACE=ci-test-$(date +%s)
terraform init -backend-config="workspace=$TF_WORKSPACE"
terraform apply -auto-approve
# run a smoke test against deployed resource (e.g., create small k8s pod)
# destroy when done
terraform destroy -auto-approve
```

Appendix B — Quick commands and diagnostics

- Check GPU node status: `kubectl get nodes -l accelerator=nvidia -o wide`
- Inspect running GPU pods: `kubectl top pod --containers -n serving`
- View recent Terraform runs: Terraform Cloud workspace -> Runs -> latest plan

Appendix C — Useful links and docs

- Terraform module registry: git@github.com:redwood/terraform-modules (internal)
- GPU fleet runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
